# Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape {.unnumbered}

A hiring committee is about to vote. Everyone has read the applications, yet the discussion turns on different things: one member remembers an impressive interview, another worries about reliability, and a third keeps returning to the candidate they liked first. Before asking who should get the job, we need to understand how these judgments took shape.

This part begins with a standard for a good decision: identify the feasible alternatives, consider their consequences, and clarify what matters. It then follows the actual process, from the evidence that attracts attention to the interpretation, expectations, and values that make one option seem preferable. The hiring case develops along the way, while a choice between job offers shows how to construct alternatives and investigate an uncertainty that could change the decision.

The distinction between predicting an outcome and valuing it will be useful throughout the book. Two people can agree about what is likely to happen and still reasonably prefer different actions.

![A reading route through Part I. The arrows show the progression of questions in this part.](../figures/master-loop-part-1.svg){fig-alt="Three reading questions: What is the decision? How does the judgment form? What can we learn afterward?"}

## Questions to carry forward

- What has shaped the choice before the vote begins?
- Are we disagreeing about what will happen, what matters, or what is possible?
- What should we record now so that the outcome can teach us later?

Once we can see how a judgment forms, we can ask how well it handles uncertainty. Part II follows the shortcuts that help us judge quickly—and the checks that reveal when they mislead.
